title: Protected domains and the cost of cooperation on weighted networks
abstract: A costly inherited trait can spread when its descendants create a favorable local environment. We ask which finite contact structures sustain such a collective competitor and what their advantage costs. Individuals play a donation game, conferring benefit $b$ at cost $c$. Reciprocal weighted contacts determine averaged payoffs and copying recipients, while sources are chosen globally according to payoff. Cooperation is favored when a uniformly introduced cooperator takes over more often than a defector in the complementary experiment. Exact fluctuation response and elimination of fast configurations identify the formation and competition of protected domains as the controlling processes. The sharp weak-selection threshold infima are $b/c=3$ on the four-cycle, $7$ on the five-site path, and $1$ on every fixed path with at least six sites. On the six-site path, a global bound forces near-barrier designs into this domain hierarchy. Polynomial relations among the contact ratios then control unrestricted optimization and imply eventual exact reflection symmetry. Reaching threshold $1+ε$ requires minimum contact contrast $656ε^{-2}[1+O(ε)]$ and neutral absorption time of order $ε^{-1}$. We determine their tradeoff and the associated design tolerance. Finite selection consumes the same margin. Within the controlled small-selection window, the maximal fixation advantage is of order $ε^{5/2}$ when the contrast exceeds its exact minimum by order $ε^{-1}$. Thus an improving invasion threshold can require increasing contact heterogeneity, precision and observation time.
summary: This work analyzes the conditions for the spread of costly cooperation on weighted networks by modeling a donation game. It derives sharp mathematical thresholds for the benefit-to-cost ratio required for cooperation to invade. The methodology uses advanced techniques from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics to quantify the structural requirements for collective traits to persist against natural selection.
main_problem: The paper investigates the conditions under which costly cooperation can spread and persist within a population structured on a weighted network.
main_result: It determines sharp weak-selection thresholds for cooperation, finding specific ratios of benefit to cost ($b/c$) required for fixation on different network structures like cycles and paths.
method: The analysis employs techniques from non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, including fluctuation response, first-passage time calculations, and optimization over network weights.
model_or_system: The model is a donation game played on a finite, weighted, undirected graph where traits (cooperator/defector) are inherited via copying based on weighted contacts.
key_observables: Weak-selection threshold ($b/c$), fixation advantage ($\Delta$), and the minimal contact contrast required for a given threshold.
important_parameters: The selection strength ($\epsilon$), the benefit ($b$), the cost ($c$), and the network topology (e.g., $C_4, P_5, P_6$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to the source-first, averaged-payoff process, and comparisons are made between individual payoff dominance and population-level fixation advantage.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate small supports, showing the minimal promoter structures for cooperation on a four-cycle ($C_4$), five-site path ($P_5$), and six-site path ($P_6$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the game and dynamics on weighted networks, to calculating fixation probabilities and susceptibility, and finally performing rigorous optimization to find the minimal structural requirements for sustained cooperation.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing the emergence of cooperation via selection thresholds on complex networks connects concepts from statistical physics (non-equilibrium dynamics, critical phenomena) to evolutionary game theory.

Filled sites are dynamically protected pins, not fixed external spins. The limits are q →∞, q2/Q →0 on C4; 1 ≪q ≪A ≪Q on P5; and q →∞, q/Q →0 on P6. The six-site construction extends to every fixed longer path.
